bp: This paper is about a common Web decision that cannot safely be reduced to a single label. A moderation system may need to decide whether a post is hate speech, spam, self-harm content, or allowed speech. A fraud system may need to decide whether a transaction is clean, suspicious, stolen-card behavior, or account takeover. In these settings, the useful answer is not only the top choice. The operator needs to know how much belief should be placed on every possible class, because the next action depends on the size and spread of that uncertainty. A language model can often explain why a record looks suspicious or harmless, especially when the record mixes ordinary text with structured fields. But the abstract says these models are not naturally good at producing calibrated multi-class probability distributions. The paper therefore serves systems that want the model's reasoning and its uncertainty at the same time, especially where overconfident mistakes are costly.
wh: The hard part is that explanation and measured uncertainty pull in different directions. If one asks a model to reason step by step, the model may produce a persuasive account but still attach unreliable chances to the possible labels. If one instead uses methods that try to force clean probability numbers out of the model, the abstract says they can sacrifice chain-of-thought reasoning, meaning the system loses the readable path that made the answer inspectable. Standard reinforcement learning for classification has another problem: the reward can be too coarse. If the model only hears that the final class was right or wrong, it receives little guidance about near misses. Predicting fraud with 45 percent belief when the expert says 55 percent is different from predicting 2 percent, but a hard reward may treat both as simply wrong. The task is also broad: the paper trains across many tabular tasks and tests on mixed structured-and-text Web data.
naive: A smart beginner might ask the language model for a label, then ask it to add confidence scores for all classes. That keeps the interface simple and appears to solve the problem: the model explains itself and prints numbers. The failure is that printed confidence is not automatically calibrated. A model can sound sure because its wording is fluent, not because the evidence supports that much certainty. Another beginner approach is to train a separate expert tabular model for each task and use that model's probabilities. That may give better measured chances on tables, but it does not naturally handle free text together with fields, and it does not give the same general reasoning ability across new tasks with only a few examples.
ap: The paper's central move is to train the language model to speak in two coordinated outputs: a readable chain of reasoning and a complete probability distribution expressed in words. A probability distribution means that belief is spread across all possible labels instead of being placed only on the winning label. The training signal comes from expert tabular models that provide soft probabilities. Soft probabilities are useful because they say more than right or wrong: they show whether an example is nearly tied, clearly one class, or partly plausible under several classes. RLVP uses those expert probability patterns as a dense reward curriculum, so the model receives fine-grained guidance while learning. The idea is not to make the model merely imitate an expert table model forever. It is to use many tabular tasks to teach a single model the habit of calibrated uncertainty while preserving its ability to explain and to generalize to heterogeneous Web tasks.
mech: The mechanism starts with classification examples from many structured tasks. Each example has input fields, possible class labels, and an expert tabular model's soft probability estimate over those labels. The language model is fine-tuned so that, when it sees a case, it first produces an interpretable chain of thought and then produces a full verbalized probability distribution. The reward is not a single checkmark for naming the right class. Instead, the expert model's soft probabilities give a graded target. If the expert believes class A is likely but class B remains possible, the training signal can reward an answer that preserves that shape of uncertainty more than one that collapses everything into one overconfident class. This addresses the insufficient reward granularity problem named in the abstract: the model gets more information per example about how wrong or right its belief spread is. Across 169 tabular tasks, the same model repeatedly sees how different evidence patterns should translate into different levels of confidence. After joint training, it is tested in few-shot settings on unseen Web benchmarks that mix structured data with free text. The output is a classification answer with reasoning and a probability distribution, intended to be useful for downstream decisions that need both an explanation and calibrated uncertainty.
math: The main mathematical object is a probability distribution: a set of chances assigned across all classes, with the total belief spread over the available answers. In plain terms, the model is not saying only "fraud" or "not fraud"; it is dividing its belief among the labels so a human or automated policy can see whether the case is obvious or borderline. Calibration is the next idea. A system is calibrated when its stated confidence matches long-run reality: among many cases where it says about 70 percent, roughly seven out of ten should turn out that way. Reinforcement learning here means training by reward, where the model tries outputs, receives a score, and adjusts its behavior toward outputs that score better. The important twist is reward granularity. A coarse reward says only winner or loser. A dense reward gives a smoother scale, because the expert probability vector contains partial credit and degrees of uncertainty. The expert tabular model acts like a teacher that has learned patterns in structured columns. The tradeoff is calibration versus reasoning: the paper tries to keep the explanatory chain while adding disciplined probability behavior. It also faces generality versus task specificity: one model trained jointly must learn reusable uncertainty habits without depending on a custom model for every new task.
dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of several recurring conference ideas. It is part of LLM calibration because it treats a language model's confidence as something that must be measured against future correctness, not accepted from fluent text. It is also part of reinforcement learning because the model is steered by rewards, but the reward is made richer by expert probability distributions rather than a single final label. It connects to Web classification work in moderation and fraud detection, where the real pressure is not leaderboard accuracy alone but deciding when to block, review, warn, or ignore. It also touches the broader probability family in the repo: many papers need to act with partial sight, and this one asks how a model should admit that uncertainty while still giving a human-readable reason. Finally, it connects to heterogeneous data work, because the abstract emphasizes settings where structured fields and free text appear together.
ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it teaches the model the shape of uncertainty, not just the name of the answer. If a training example is ambiguous, the expert probabilities can show that ambiguity directly. The model can then learn that similar evidence should produce a spread-out answer rather than a confident winner. If an example is clear, the teacher distribution can reward concentrated belief. Repeating this over many tabular tasks gives the model many small lessons about how field patterns relate to calibrated confidence. Preserving the reasoning path matters because mixed Web cases often need interpretation: a text description and a set of structured fields may support different parts of the decision. The reasoning can organize that evidence, while the verbalized probability distribution tells the downstream system how sharply to act. The abstract's few-shot claim is plausible under this logic: if the model has learned a general discipline for mapping evidence strength to probability, it may need fewer examples on a new task than a task-specific expert model trained from scratch.
po: The payoff is a classifier that can be used where both explanation and uncertainty matter. According to the abstract, a single RLVP-trained model is trained jointly on 169 tabular tasks, surpasses a strong task-specific XGBoost baseline on up to 55 percent of those tasks, and shows strong few-shot performance on unseen heterogeneous Web benchmarks mixing structured data and free text. In practical terms, the system buys a more inspectable decision surface: it can say why it leans toward a class and how much belief remains for alternatives, which is valuable for moderation, fraud review, and other high-stakes Web decisions.
limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. The approach depends on expert tabular models producing useful soft probabilities; if those teachers are biased, poorly calibrated, or blind to text-based evidence, the reward can pass those weaknesses to the language model. The abstract reports results across many tasks, but the input excerpt is cut off, so it does not fully state the evaluation details, class definitions, or failure cases. Verbalized probabilities also require reliable parsing and interpretation by downstream systems. The method assumes that calibration habits learned from 169 tabular tasks transfer to unseen mixed Web tasks, which may fail when new domains use different signals, labels, user behavior, or risk thresholds.
